clue.text: Poss iffy rug?

indicators.note: the question mark is the only signal here: it flags the words as an iffy, questionable version of something else to be rearranged

parts.note: these words are taken letter for letter as the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone eyes a dubious-looking hairpiece and wonders whether it will pass.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no word signalling the scramble: only the question mark. Cockney rhyming slang shortens the answer to its first word, meaning a wig, which ties in with the puzzle's wig theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodgy rug is a poor wig, and the rhyming-slang phrase stands for wigs, besides being an old laxative.

clue.text: Stone mug (note: contents highly acidic)

indicators.note: the bracket's words are what goes inside the mug and note, so they are put within

parts.note: a mug is a fool, a sap
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
a pH of 1 is extremely acidic, so pH plus I (one)

explanation.surface: A stone mug carries a warning that what it holds is strongly acidic.
explanation.definitionFit: A sapphire is a precious stone, usually blue corundum.

clue.text: In Bern, I'm exchanging currency

indicators.note: exchanging suggests letters swapping places, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller in the Swiss capital is changing money.
explanation.definitionFit: The renminbi is the official currency of China, whose unit is the yuan.

clue.text: Heads up: Prime Minister implores Republican Party to work on image

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the picked letters are read from the bottom
the heads of these words are their initial letters

explanation.surface: A prime minister urges his party to polish its public image, with a heads-up.
explanation.definitionFit: To primp is to groom oneself fussily, improving one's appearance.

clue.text: How to get foie gras on the menu in the NAAFI?

definitions.text: How to get foie gras on the menu in the NAAFI?

parts.words: How to get foie gras on the menu in the NAAFI?
parts.note: foie gras comes from geese fed by tube; the NAAFI runs canteens for the armed forces, so its food is the forces' feed

explanation.surface: A question about putting a luxury French delicacy on a military canteen menu.
explanation.walkthrough: The NAAFI is the organisation running shops and canteens for the British armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Geese are crammed with grain to fatten their livers for foie gras, and read in two words it is the forces' food.

clue.text: Photo journal that is in circulation

indicators.note: the letters for that is go round the journal, encircling it

parts.note: a magazine, a mag

explanation.surface: A picture from a magazine that is currently in circulation.
explanation.definitionFit: A photograph is a picture, an image.

clue.text: Not happy to eat Delia's tossed leaves

indicators.note: one word swallowing others puts them inside it

parts.note: unhappy means sad

indicators.note: tossed like a salad, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Someone glum is made to eat the leaves Delia has tossed.
explanation.walkthrough: Delia Smith is a famous British TV cook.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bowl of salad leaves served alongside a main course is a kind of leaves dish.

clue.text: Stocked by Tesco, Dr Oetker's ingredient for taramasalata

indicators.note: the letters are stocked inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A supermarket and a food brand carry an ingredient for a Greek dip.
explanation.definitionFit: Taramasalata is a dip traditionally made from fish eggs, often those of the cod.

clue.text: For going on the floor, reprimand Rover (dog, possibly)

parts.note: Rover is a British car make
a dog is one example of a pet

explanation.surface: Someone tells off their dog Rover for messing on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For going on the floor' is a second definition: a carpet goes on the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone, in British usage, is to summon them for a dressing-down, as onto the boss's carpet.

clue.text: Male lecturer given a lethal dosage

parts.note: a university lecturer is a don
LD is the pharmacologist's abbreviation for lethal dose

explanation.surface: A man teaching at a university is given a fatal dose.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a man's first name, so a male person may bear it.

clue.text: Gutless pilferer snatching little girl's breadbasket

indicators.note: the outer letters grab the girl and hold her between them
with its insides gone the word keeps only its outer letters

parts.note: Annie, as in Little Orphan Annie

explanation.surface: A cowardly thief grabs a little girl's basket of bread.
explanation.definitionFit: A pannier is a large basket, such as one for carrying loaves.

clue.text: A new Rodin sculpture, reportedly part of The Great Exhibition?

definitions.text: reportedly part of The Great Exhibition

indicators.note: a sculpture reshapes material, so the name is remoulded

explanation.surface: A newly made Rodin statue is said to have been shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' turns Great into grate: the definition is a part of a grate on display.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedogs are a pair of iron supports for logs in a grate, a fitting by the hearth.

clue.text: Musical composition is a bit over the top

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
a musical composition is a piece

explanation.surface: A piece of music is judged rather overdone.
explanation.definitionFit: A wig worn on top of the head is literally a bit placed over the top.

clue.text: Grow louder, like Cole Porter's party?

definitions.meaning: the Cole Porter song 'Well, Did You Evah!' has the line 'What a ... party this is'

explanation.definitionFit: To increase in volume is a standard verb sense, and the adjective means splendid, as in Porter's lyric.

clue.text: Pull Nicolas' leg — it's quite bony!

parts.note: to pull someone's leg is to tease, to rib them
Nicolas Cage is the Hollywood actor

explanation.surface: Someone plays a practical joke on a film star, or teases him about his skinny leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull ... leg' together give RIB, with the actor's surname in between.
explanation.definitionFit: The chest's framework of curved bones round heart and lungs is thoroughly bony.

clue.text: Rabbit's head in Bechamel perhaps a treat for Tiddles?

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the description of the sauce

parts.note: béchamel is a white sauce made with ...

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A rabbit's head cooked in white sauce might please a pet cat.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiddles is a stock British name for a pet cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat is traditionally given a shallow dish of something white and creamy as a treat.

clue.text: See 14
Blackfriars theatre screening Spielberg classic -she'll give you a ticket!

indicators.note: the theatre screens, or shows, the film within itself

parts.note: the Mermaid Theatre stands at Blackfriars in London
E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film

explanation.surface: A London theatre shows a Spielberg film, and an usher hands out tickets.
explanation.definitionFit: A female traffic warden issues parking tickets to drivers who overstay.

clue.text: Bobby Charlton's parting shot: Gone With The Wind?

definitions.text: Bobby Charlton's parting shot: Gone With The Wind?

parts.words: Bobby Charlton's parting shot: Gone With The Wind?
parts.note: the footballer Bobby Charlton was famous for long strands of hair swept across his bald pate from a low parting, which blew loose in the wind

explanation.surface: A footballer's final goal is likened to an epic film title.
explanation.walkthrough: Bobby Charlton was an England and Manchester United football star.
explanation.definitionFit: The hairstyle sweeps strands from a low side parting over a bald crown, and wind can lift them off.

clue.text: Becomes reacquainted with tragedy during Sir Christopher's decapitation

indicators.note: the tragedy sits within the beheaded name
losing its head means the first letter goes

parts.note: Sir Christopher Wren, architect of St Paul's, in the possessive
King Lear is Shakespeare's tragedy

explanation.surface: Someone rediscovers tragedy while an architect is beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick up again knowledge once lost is to come back to familiarity with it.

clue.text: Like The Eagles? Only some, to be blunt

definitions.meaning: only some eagles, such as the American national bird, are described with this word for hairless-headed
plain and unadorned, as a statement made without softening

explanation.definitionFit: A bald eagle has a white head, and a bald statement is frank and unvarnished.

clue.text: Naughtily adopt the French "frog" at a young age

indicators.note: behaving naughtily, the letters misbehave and rearrange

parts.note: le is French for the

explanation.surface: A naughty adoption of a French frog at a tender age.
explanation.definitionFit: The larva of a frog, with tail and gills, is its juvenile stage.

clue.text: He sells bonds to raise money for child-king

definitions.text: He sells bonds to raise money

parts.note: offspring are issue
R is the abbreviation for rex, king

explanation.surface: A financier sells bonds to fund a boy king.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrower who puts out bonds for sale offers them to investors as the body that creates them.

clue.text: Old printer driver's support is about to offer patchy coverage

indicators.note: the tee goes around the printer's letters

parts.note: a golfer's driver strikes a ball resting on a tee
OUP, Oxford University Press, one of the oldest printers

explanation.surface: An old printing machine's driver has a support that gives uneven coverage.
explanation.definitionFit: A wig covering a bald patch gives partial, sometimes unconvincing coverage of the scalp.

clue.text: Knut's grabbed by drunken Scot; one shouldn't grumble really

indicators.note: the setter is held inside the scrambled letters
drunk, the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: Knut is the setter, so 'Knut's' is 'I is'

explanation.surface: The setter is seized by a drunken Scotsman but shouldn't really complain.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who bears hardship without complaint is a philosophical endurer.

clue.text: Where North, South, East and West meet?

definitions.text: Where North, South, East and West meet?

parts.words: Where North, South, East and West meet?
parts.note: in bridge the four players are named after compass points and sit round a small square table

explanation.surface: A geography question about the meeting place of the four compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridge players are called North, South, East and West and gather round a folding table for their game.

clue.text: Madonna lost 90% of capital, having to beg

indicators.note: the capital letter M, Roman 1000, keeps only a tenth of its value and becomes Roman 100

parts.note: Madge is the British tabloid nickname for the singer Madonna

explanation.surface: A pop star loses almost all her money and is reduced to begging.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrounge or ask for something free is to sponge, the sense of the verb.

clue.text: Mostly honest politician's quite a card

indicators.note: most of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: honest means true
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A mostly honest politician is quite a character.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games a trump is a card of the suit ranked above the rest.

clue.text: Stood up, I'm terribly embarrassed

indicators.note: done terribly, the letters fall out of order

parts.note: an embarrassed face goes red

explanation.surface: Someone stood up, perhaps on a date, is mortified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stood up' looks like one phrase; 'Stood' alone is the definition and 'up' joins the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand in a match is to officiate as its referee, so stood is the past tense.

clue.text: Associate leading Archer's case "trembling with excitement"

indicators.note: the first piece goes in front of the second

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for associate, as in ACA
an archer keeps arrows in a quiver

explanation.surface: A colleague introduces an archer's legal case with breathless excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: Quivering all over with eagerness is the state of being all of a tremble.

clue.text: See 7
WC left first hint of slurry; green wellies a must here

parts.note: W. C. Fields, the American comedian
port is the left side of a ship

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A rural toilet, the smell of slurry, and rubber boots essential.
explanation.walkthrough: Green wellies are rubber boots worn by the British country set.
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting, hunting and fishing are outdoor country pursuits where rubber boots are standard.
